findings.title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so a code can be used twice or resurrected
findings.body: The new backup-code login branch decrypts `user.backupCodes` into an array, nulls the matched entry (`backupCodes[index] = null`) and then writes the whole re-encrypted array back with `prisma.user.update`. This is a read-modify-write with no transaction or conditional update. Two login requests that arrive concurrently with the same code both match it and both return success, so the "each backup code can be used exactly once" guarantee advertised in `backup_code_instructions` is not enforced. Worse, two concurrent requests with *different* codes each write back a list derived from the same original snapshot, so the last write wins and the code consumed by the other request is silently restored and becomes reusable. Because an attacker typically does not need parallelism, this is not trivially exploitable, but the single-use property of a security credential must hold under concurrency. Suggested fix: perform the removal atomically (e.g. a `updateMany` guarded on the exact previous encrypted value, or a transaction with a row lock / `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`), or store codes as individual rows and delete by id/`deleteMany`.

findings.title: onEnable is only fired from the backup-codes Close button, so dismissing the dialog otherwise leaves 2FA state stale
findings.body: Before this change `onEnable()` was called as soon as the enable API returned 200. Now enablement is only reported to the parent from the `backup-codes-close` button (`resetState(); onEnable();`). The dialog is controlled by the parent and Radix closes it on Escape (and on other dismissal paths) via `onOpenChange`, none of which call `onEnable` or `resetState`. Consequence: a user who enables 2FA and closes the dialog with Escape gets a server state where 2FA is enabled, while the settings page still shows the toggle as unchecked; if they retry, `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup` answers `TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled` and they get a generic "something went wrong" error. The internal `step` also stays on `DisplayBackupCodes`, so re-opening the modal later shows the old backup-code screen instead of the password step. `onEnable` should be invoked (and state reset) whenever the dialog is dismissed after a successful enable, not only from one button.

findings.title: Backup-code input is not normalized, so auto-capitalized or whitespace-pasted codes are rejected
findings.body: The new backup-code input is a plain `TextField` with no `autoCapitalize="none"`/`autoCorrect="off"`/`spellCheck={false}`. Codes are generated as lowercase hex (`crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`) and the server-side match is an exact, case-sensitive `array.indexOf(value)` after only stripping `-` (`next-auth-options.ts:144` and `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts:61`). On mobile (and iOS Safari in particular) a text input auto-capitalizes the first character, so typing the code shown on screen produces a mismatch and "Backup code is incorrect" — precisely in the lost-access recovery path where the user has no other way in. Pasting a code with surrounding whitespace fails for the same reason. Add the input attributes and/or `trim()`/`toLowerCase()` the value before comparing.

findings.title: missing_backup_codes message tells users to generate codes in settings, which is impossible
findings.body: The new `missing_backup_codes` string reads "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." but no such setting exists: backup codes are only produced by `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup`, which returns `TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled` for any user who already has 2FA on, and there is no UI to regenerate them. Every user who enabled 2FA before this migration (`backupCodes` is `NULL`) and then clicks "Lost access" will follow the advice, find nothing, and be stuck. Either provide a regenerate-codes entry point in the 2FA settings section or change the text to describe what the user can actually do (e.g. disable and re-enable 2FA).

findings.title: No test covers logging in with a backup code or its single-use behaviour
findings.body: The PR's core security behaviours are untested. The added assertions only verify that the download produces a file named `cal-backup-codes.txt`, that the copy button shows a toast, and that Close works (`// TODO: check file content`, `// TODO: check clipboard content`), and a `// TODO: add more backup code tests` is left behind. Nothing exercises: logging in via "Lost access" with a real code, rejection of a wrong code, the fact that a consumed code cannot be reused (the guarantee the UI copy makes), or disabling 2FA with a backup code. Since the consumption logic lives in `next-auth-options.ts` and is exactly the part that can silently regress (including the concurrency issue above), at least a happy-path login-with-backup-code test and a reuse-rejection test should be added before merge.

findings.title: New `required` on the password field blocks disabling 2FA for accounts with no password
findings.body: `required` was added to the password `PasswordField`. The field is rendered whenever the caller doesn't pass `disablePassword` (the default), and the API deliberately treats the password as optional: `disable.ts` only verifies it `if (user.password && user.identityProvider === IdentityProvider.CAL)`. Accounts that have 2FA enabled but no password (e.g. a user who set up 2FA while using CAL credentials and later signed in with Google, which nulls `password`, or SAML/Google accounts with 2FA) can legitimately disable 2FA server-side, but the browser now refuses to submit the form with an empty required field, so they are blocked in the UI. The client-side constraint should mirror the server rule (e.g. only mark it required when the account actually has a password).

findings.title: Third-party identity-provider guard makes backup codes unusable for OAuth accounts with 2FA
findings.body: The existing guard `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode) throw new Error(ErrorCode.ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled)` runs before the new backup-code branch. A user with a GOOGLE/SAML identity provider who has 2FA enabled necessarily submits a backup code with an empty `totpCode`, so they always hit this error and can never use their backup codes, even though `loginWithTotp` routes such users through the 2FA login page. Either the guard should also accept a supplied `backupCode`, or the limitation should be made explicit (and the UI should not offer a path that can never succeed) — as written, the feature silently does not apply to that group of 2FA users.
